content:
I am a huge Sonos fan and user, having been hooked since the original Sonos Ace launched. So when I heard about two years ago that Sonos was entering the over-ear headphone space, I knew I had to try them. The Sonos Ace looked great, felt great, and brought some excellent Sonos ecosystem features. But as a pair of high-end headphones, there were a few things I felt were lacking — the bass wasn't strong enough, the active noise cancellation was just okay, and the app experience could be better. Now, however, the new Sonos Ace Ultra feels like it has ticked off most of the complaints from customers (including mine) one by one. I've spent nearly a month with them, using them as my primary headphones for travel, video editing, working out, walking around, and just everyday listening. So I know them well, and here's what you need to know.

Be sure to check out our Sonos Ace Ultra hands-on video below:

At first glance, the Sonos Ace Ultra doesn't look all that different from the original Sonos Ace. Sonos has kept the same clean, understated design, only shifting a few of the chrome accents around and adding a couple of new colours. But the biggest differences are actually on the inside.

What's different from the original Sonos Ace

Here are some of the biggest changes from the original Sonos Ace to the Ace Ultra:

  • Redesigned 40mm drivers
  • A 10-microphone array, up from 8 on the original
  • An improved adaptive active noise cancellation that is claimed to be up to 2x better, and can dynamically adjust to changes with glasses, hair, and earcup seal
  • Longer battery life of up to 35 hours with active noise cancellation on
  • Bluetooth 6.0, up from 5.4
  • Expanded EQ controls with three presets and advanced 8-band EQ options
  • Headphones can connect to the Sonos ecosystem
  • User-replaceable battery
  • Updated earcup and headband padding materials
  • Earcups can rotate further, allowing them to lay flat when worn around the neck
  • Two new colours: Agave and Sand

Of these changes, the main differences I've noticed are the re-tuned acoustic performance, better bass response, and stronger active noise cancellation. With the original Sonos Ace, I would sometimes hear a 'hiss' when noise cancellation was enabled. It didn't happen often, but I definitely noticed it. The Sonos Ace Ultra has fixed that issue. You still get some of the standout specs from the previous generation, including:

  • Spatial audio and Dolby Atmos
  • Dynamic head tracking
  • Lossless audio playback on supported devices
  • USB-C and 3.5mm wired audio input
  • Bluetooth multipoint connection
  • Quick charging: 3 minutes of charging provides up to 3 hours of playback
  • TV Audio Swap compatibility with Sonos speakers

They retain the same high-quality build, blending plastic and metal for a premium, lightweight feel. The Sonos Ace Ultra continues with magnetic, swappable earcups, and one of my personal favourite additions is the new EQ settings, which let me dial in my preferred sound more precisely. But as an everyday headphone, how does it actually perform?

User experience

Specs look great on paper, but what impresses me most about the Ace Ultra is that the sound quality has clearly improved. My biggest complaint about the original Sonos Ace was the lack of bass depth. The bass wasn't bad, but for a $450 product, I felt it left something to be desired. I listen to a lot of R&B, hip-hop, and pop, so bass matters a lot to me. I wanted more thump and to feel that impact. The Ace Ultra finally delivers the experience I was after.

The low end has noticeably more impact and depth. But importantly, Sonos hasn't simply 'turned up' the bass. Any headphone brand can boost bass — the challenge is maintaining sound separation so the low end doesn't drown out vocals, instruments, and high frequencies. That's exactly where the Ace Ultra impresses me. The bass is stronger, yet vocals remain clear, bright, and easy to listen to. It's not just music either — everything sounds better across all media, including podcasts, movies, and all the YouTube videos I watch. The sound performance is excellent across every type of media.

The improved active noise cancellation is also an immediately noticeable upgrade. The new 10-microphone array allows more sounds to be dynamically blocked out. Even without any media playing, the headphones get absurdly quiet in many different environments. Almost too good to be true! The biggest improvement in noise cancellation is handling sudden, unexpected noises. Blocking out constant noise like aeroplane engines is one thing, but being able to block out passing cars, construction noise, sirens, or sudden loud sounds while walking around is another matter entirely.

Finally, two things worth mentioning: comfort and the Sonos ecosystem. These are the most comfortable headphones I've ever worn. Even on long-haul flights lasting 8 to 10 hours, I kept them on about 95% of the time without any soreness, discomfort, or stuffiness. Lastly, I have lots of Sonos speakers in my home, and they've added a feature that lets you one-tap transfer music from the speakers to the headphones. It's a great feature, but I personally don't use it all that much.

My only complaint is that the case needs a new zipper or clasp design, because the sticker keeps sticking to things and gets really annoying!

Pricing and availability

The Sonos Ace Ultra is available starting today on Sonos.com and Amazon for $449, the same launch price as the original Sonos Ace. It comes in four colours: Black, White, Agave, and Sand. I've also spotted the original Sonos Ace on Amazon for $239 while supplies last. At that $240 price point, it's still a solid option.

At its $450 price point, the Sonos Ace Ultra firmly sits in the high-end noise-cancelling headphone category, going head-to-head with offerings from Apple, Bose, and Sony.

The verdict

The original Sonos Ace felt like a solid first-generation product. The Sonos Ace Ultra feels like a complete, refined product. As we've seen, not much has changed on the outside or in design, but improvements have been made everywhere that matters, with a few new useful features thrown in as well. The sound is noticeably better, noise cancellation is stronger and smarter, battery life is longer, the app experience is smoother, and the Agave green is absolutely gorgeous.

If you already own the original Sonos Ace, I think this upgrade is absolutely worth it, depending on what features you prioritise. If you're looking to buy a pair of high-end headphones right now, the Sonos Ace Ultra should absolutely be on your shortlist. $449 isn't cheap by any means, but if you want one of the best high-end headphones out there and you're already a Sonos fan, you're going to love these.
